supporters.quote: 'significant sustained effects on cognitive flexibility (2 studies, g = 4.28, 95 % CI: 1.82–6.73, p < 0.01), inhibitory control (3 studies, g = 2.43, 95 % CI: 0.25–4.60, p = 0.029), attention (6 studies, g = 1.62, 95 % CI: 0.31–2.93, p = 0.02), and visuospatial ability (2 studies, g = 5.60, 95 % CI: 4.50–6.70, p < 0.001).' (p. 6); 'Leave-one-out influence analyses further demonstrated stability for both modalities: trTMS remained robust (g = 0.37–0.42; overall 0.40 [0.24–0.56]) with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 47 %)' (p. 4); 'because this evidence derives from different groups within a single study (Benussi et al., 2020), additional studies are needed to confirm this effect.' (p. 10)
supporters.note: Mixed MCI and dementia review (80 RCTs, 23 on MCI). The extreme magnitudes the ledger cites (g 4.28 and 5.60) are two-'study' pools of 46/24 participants (Table 4), the same sample as the sustained tDCS 'other dementia' pool (Table 2) that the authors attribute to groups within one frontotemporal dementia study (Benussi 2020): they are neither MCI evidence nor two independent trials. In the MCI subgroups the effects are moderate and heterogeneous (trTMS g = 0.77, 5 trials, I2 = 63%; tDCS g = 0.72, 9 trials, I2 = 63%; Table 2). The review also reports a robust, high-certainty small short-term trTMS effect on global cognition (g = 0.40, I2 = 47%, stable across sensitivity and leave-one-out analyses), which contradicts 'no stable effect size emerges for any class' for mixed MCI and dementia samples. Supports the large-but-heterogeneous pattern for tDCS pools (I2 77 to 95%, tACS 97%) and the fragility of the MCI subgroup estimates only.

supporters.quote: 'the rTMS-F3F4 (SMD =1.52[95 %CIs =0.49–2.56]) and rTMS-F3 (SMD =1.25[95 %CIs =0.57–1.93]) significantly enhanced the global cognition function impact in comparison with sham stimulation.' (p. 3); 'the overall quality of evidence of the overall NMA, direct and indirect evidence, was low to medium.' (p. 5); 'First, this NMA may have been underpowered because of the heterogeneity of the participants [...] Second, although all the trials included a sham stimulation in their study design, they may not have been adequately blinded because of differences in the interventions used. Third, given the relatively small number of RCTs (and by extension patients) included' (p. 7)
supporters.note: MCI-only network meta-analysis of NIBS (19 RCTs, 599 participants; the global-cognition network is 16 RCTs, 532 participants spread over 8 nodes). Large SMDs with wide intervals, GRADE low to medium, possible unblinding, weak network geometry, self-described as possibly underpowered. No I2 is reported (heterogeneity given as tau, with 'significant differences' in some comparisons); Egger non-significant. The MoCA mean difference of 5.59 points for bilateral DLPFC rTMS is very large for an MCI screening scale. Shares trials with P-520 (Padala 2018, Yuan 2021, Drumond Marra 2015) and overlaps the MCI subset of P-373, so it is not an independent trial corpus.

supporters.quote: 'All outcome indicators used for the evaluation of cognitive function in all trials were combined.' (p. 6); 'rTMS treatment exerted a significant effect on cognition in patients with MCI (SMD = 0.83, 95% CI = 0.44–1.22), with [...] moderate between-study heterogeneity (I2 = 65%, Figure 4).' (pp. 6 to 8); 'the heterogeneity of included studies was high (I2 = 71%, p = 0.0004)' (p. 8); 'First, the number of studies included and sample size were small.' (p. 13)
supporters.note: rTMS in MCI only (12 RCTs, 329 patients, arms of 8 to 25). Heterogeneity 65% overall and 71% for global cognition, but 26% for memory. Pools MoCA, MMSE and memory and executive test scores as a single SMD and includes single-session trials. The authors conclude rTMS is 'safe and effective' and do not call the estimate fragile, but they report the elements the statement lists (few small trials, I2 65 to 71%, heterogeneous scales pooled as SMD). Same intervention class as P-373 and P-461, with overlapping trials.

supporters.quote: '(g=0.978; 95% CI, 0.298-1.659; P<.05; figure 4A). There was no publication bias (Egger test P=.303), but considerable heterogeneity was found (Q=8; I2=93%).' (p. 13); 'we included a considerable number of studies with very small sample sizes, which may increase the risk of type I error and inflate the effect sizes' (p. 14)
supporters.note: Multicomponent exercise in mixed MCI and dementia; the MCI global-cognition pool is 10 trials, 384 participants, mixing MMSE, ADAS-Cog and MoCA. The MCI executive-function estimate was driven by one small study (Silva study 1, g = 2.103) and fell from 0.605 to 0.448 when it was removed. Three MCI trials (refs 48, 49, 51: Doi, Makizako, Suzuki) list identical N = 50 and identical baseline MMSE and age in Table 1, suggesting one cohort may enter the pool more than once (an observation from the table, not stated by the authors). The only exercise-class supporter.

supporters.quote: 'CCT2x demonstrated statistically significant improvements in global cognitive function (SMD, 1.21 [95 % CI, 0.69–1.73])' (p. 1); 'Sample sizes varied from 19 to 117 participants.' (p. 4); 'Given the limited sample sizes from 10 RCTs, statistical power may also be an issue' (p. 7). Searched for 'fragile' and 'thin': not present in the source.
supporters.note: Mobile computerised cognitive training NMA, 10 RCTs mixing MCI, dementia, subjective memory complaint and subclinical decline. The 'CCT2x' node includes an 'active use' arm defined by days of app use (Robert 2020, active MeMo users), which is not a randomised contrast. Heterogeneity is acknowledged but no I2 is reported; Egger non-significant; the authors call their synthesis 'the highest level of evidence' and conclude CCT is effective. The ledger's 'self-described thin and fragile' is not the paper's wording. Supports only a weaker form: a large pooled SMD from few small trials with acknowledged heterogeneity and limited power.

narrowed_wording: In three intervention classes (non-invasive brain stimulation, multicomponent exercise, computerised cognitive training), the meta-analyses reviewed report moderate-to-large pooled effects on cognition in MCI (SMD about 0.8 to 1.5) that rest on few small trials, with substantial heterogeneity where it is reported (I2 about 63 to 93%) and different cognitive scales pooled as SMDs, so none gives a precise, harmonised MCI effect size. The brain-stimulation syntheses share trials; the largest magnitudes (g 4.3 to 5.6) come from two-study pools in non-MCI dementia samples; and one synthesis reports a stable small short-term rTMS effect (g = 0.40) in mixed MCI and dementia samples.
reasoning: Three supporters answer yes (P-461, P-520, P-603) and two partly (P-373, P-655), so the count bar is met, but only from two intervention classes (brain stimulation twice, exercise once), and the two stimulation meta-analyses share trials (Padala 2018, Yuan 2021, Drumond Marra 2015), contrary to the record's 'distinct trial corpora per meta-analysis'. Across all five supporters only three classes appear (stimulation three times, exercise, computerised cognitive training). Nutrition, the fourth class the ledger names, has no supporter (P-294 and P-427 are cited in the notes but are not in the supporter list), so 'four or more intervention classes' is not sustained. The 'implausible magnitudes' element rests on P-373's g 4.28 and 5.60, which are two-study pools of 46/24 participants matching the non-MCI 'other dementia' pool the authors trace to groups within a single study, so it cannot be stated as an MCI finding. 'No stable effect size emerges for any class' is contradicted for mixed MCI and dementia samples by P-373's robust high-certainty trTMS effect (g = 0.40, I2 = 47%, stable on leave-one-out); within MCI-only pools every estimate is heterogeneous, imprecise or built on few small trials, so a fragility statement confined to MCI pools is sustained. Further ledger details not borne out by the sources: P-655 does not describe itself as 'thin and fragile', and P-461 reports no I2. The Table A1 support count of 5 should read 3 full and 2 partial.
